topics.title: Egypt in Greek and Roman Eyes
topics.short: Herodotus, Diodorus and Strabo described Egypt; their accounts mix good observation with hearsay.
topics.trouble: Students treat Herodotus as an eyewitness to the pyramid age. He wrote about two thousand years after it, from what guides told him.

topics.title: A Script Forgotten
topics.short: After the 4th century AD no one could read hieroglyphs; writers like Horapollo and later Athanasius Kircher read them as pure symbols.
topics.trouble: Students think hieroglyphs were always understood as sounds. For 1,400 years scholars thought they were mystical symbols.

topics.title: Obelisks on the Move
topics.short: Romans carried obelisks to Rome, and later ones went to Paris, London and New York, spreading interest in Egypt.
topics.trouble: Students think "Cleopatra's Needles" were made for Cleopatra. They were made for Thutmose III, more than a thousand years earlier.

topics.title: Napoleon's Expedition
topics.short: Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798 with scholars who measured and drew the monuments; their Description de l'Égypte appeared from 1809.
topics.trouble: Students credit Napoleon's soldiers with deciphering hieroglyphs. They found the Rosetta Stone; reading it took another two decades.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone
topics.short: Found at Rosetta in 1799, the stone carries a decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and went to the British Museum in 1802.
topics.trouble: Students think the three texts are in three languages. There are two languages (Egyptian and Greek) in three scripts.

topics.title: Thomas Young
topics.short: Thomas Young showed that cartouches held royal names, read part of Ptolemy's name, and saw that Demotic used sound signs too (1814–1819).
topics.trouble: Students give all the credit to one man. Young made real progress; Champollion built the full system.

topics.title: Champollion's Breakthrough
topics.short: In 1822 Champollion read Ptolemy and Cleopatra, then Ramesses and Thutmose in older cartouches, and announced his results in the Lettre à M. Dacier.
topics.trouble: Students think Champollion read only Greek names. The breakthrough was reading native names like Ramesses with sound signs.

topics.title: How the Code Was Cracked
topics.short: The keys were a bilingual text, royal names that could be matched across scripts, and Coptic, which gave the sounds of Egyptian words.
topics.trouble: Students think the Greek translation alone was enough. Without Coptic, the sounds of the words would have stayed unknown.

topics.title: A Mixed System
topics.short: In his Précis (1824), Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs, word signs and determinatives.
topics.trouble: Students think hieroglyphs are an alphabet once decoded. They are a mixed system, alphabet plus much more.

topics.title: Proving It: Lepsius and the Canopus Decree
topics.short: Richard Lepsius refined the system, and the Canopus Decree, found in 1866, another bilingual text, confirmed it.
topics.trouble: Students think decipherment was accepted at once. It was argued over until new texts proved it.

topics.title: Collectors and the Antiquities Trade
topics.short: In the early 1800s adventurers like Giovanni Belzoni shipped statues to Europe; much was lost because no one recorded where things were found.
topics.trouble: Students think early collectors were archaeologists. They took objects, often with no record of their context.

topics.title: Mariette and the Antiquities Service
topics.short: Auguste Mariette founded Egypt's Antiquities Service in 1858 and a national museum at Bulaq to keep finds in Egypt.
topics.trouble: Students think all early finds left Egypt. Mariette began the effort to keep them.

topics.title: Flinders Petrie's Methods
topics.short: Petrie excavated with care from the 1880s, recording small finds and pottery, and published his results quickly.
topics.trouble: Students think only gold and statues matter. Petrie showed that broken pots can date a site.

topics.title: Seriation (Sequence Dating)
topics.short: Petrie put Predynastic graves in order by the changing styles of their pottery, giving "sequence dates" before any calendar dates existed.
topics.trouble: Students take sequence dates as years. They give an order, not a number of years.

topics.title: Stratigraphy
topics.short: Layers of soil pile up over time, so lower layers are usually older; recording layers lets archaeologists date finds by their context.
topics.trouble: Students assume the deeper layer is always older. Pits, burrows and building can mix layers.

topics.title: Carter and KV62
topics.short: In 1922 Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) and spent about ten years recording and clearing it.
topics.trouble: Students believe in a curse. Carter and most of the team lived for years; the "curse" was a newspaper story.

topics.title: Context and Recording
topics.short: An object's value to history depends on its context: where it lay, with what, in which layer. Excavation destroys a site, so records are everything.
topics.trouble: Students value objects without their findspots. An object without context has lost most of its story.

topics.title: Relative and Absolute Dates
topics.short: Relative dating puts things in order (older or younger); absolute dating gives a date in years, with a margin.
topics.trouble: Students mix the two. "Earlier than the pottery in layer 3" is relative; "c. 2500 BC" is absolute.

topics.title: Radiocarbon Dating
topics.short: Living things take in carbon-14, which decays at a known rate after death; measuring what is left dates plant and animal remains, after calibration.
topics.trouble: Students date stone with radiocarbon. It dates once-living things, like reeds, wood, seeds or linen.

topics.title: Luminescence Dating
topics.short: Thermoluminescence can date when pottery was last fired, by the light trapped energy gives off when heated.
topics.trouble: Students expect it to be as precise as radiocarbon. Its margins are usually wider.

topics.title: Dating by Texts and Styles
topics.short: Inscriptions with regnal years and royal names, and the style of objects, date finds to a reign or period.
topics.trouble: Students take a king's name on an object as proof of its date. Names could be added later, or copied.

topics.title: Recording Inscriptions
topics.short: Epigraphers copy inscriptions exactly as they are, damaged parts included; Chicago's Epigraphic Survey has worked at Luxor since 1924.
topics.trouble: Students think a photograph is enough. Light and damage hide details that careful copying recovers.

topics.title: From Tracing to 3-D Scanning
topics.short: Methods range from hand tracing checked against the wall, to photogrammetry and laser scanning.
topics.trouble: Students think new technology replaces the expert. Every method still needs a trained eye to check it.

topics.title: Brackets for Damage and Restoration
topics.short: Editions mark restored text with [ ], partly visible signs with ⸢ ⸣, and words the scribe left out with ⟨ ⟩.
topics.trouble: Students read restored words as certain. Brackets show what the editor supplied.

topics.title: Where Egyptian Objects Are
topics.short: Great collections are in Cairo (the Egyptian Museum and the Grand Egyptian Museum), London, Paris, Berlin, Turin and New York, among others.
topics.trouble: Students think every important object is in Egypt. Many of the most famous are abroad, like the Rosetta Stone in London.

topics.title: The Debate Over Returning Objects
topics.short: Some argue that famous objects taken in colonial times should go back to Egypt; others argue they were acquired legally, are well kept and seen by many. This topic sets out both sides.
topics.trouble: Students expect one obviously right answer. Each case turns on how an object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public.

topics.title: Laws on Antiquities
topics.short: Egypt's laws now keep antiquities as state property (Law 117 of 1983), and the 1970 UNESCO Convention works against illegal trade.
topics.trouble: Students think old finds and new finds are treated the same. Laws apply differently to objects that left before and after them.

topics.title: Survey from the Air and Space
topics.short: Archaeologists find and map sites with field survey, aerial photographs, satellite images and geophysics, often without digging.
topics.trouble: Students think archaeology always means digging. Much is learned without a shovel.

topics.title: Science in the Lab
topics.short: CT scans look inside mummies without unwrapping them; studies of ancient DNA, residues and isotopes are newer and still debated in places.
topics.trouble: Students take every science headline as settled. New methods need careful checking, and results are often revised.

topics.title: The Nubian Rescue
topics.short: When the Aswan High Dam was built, a UNESCO campaign (1960–1980) moved temples such as Abu Simbel and Philae and surveyed Nubia before the flood.
topics.trouble: Students think every Nubian site was saved. Many sites, and whole villages, now lie under Lake Nasser.

topics.title: Egyptian Egyptologists
topics.short: Egyptian scholars, from Ahmed Kamal and Selim Hassan in the early 1900s to today's excavators, have led the study of their own past.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptology is only a European field. Egyptians have been central to it for over a century.

topics.title: What Hieratic Is
topics.short: Hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs, written with a brush and ink, used from the earliest dynasties alongside hieroglyphs.
topics.trouble: Students think hieratic came after hieroglyphs. The two were used side by side from the beginning.

topics.title: What Was Written in Hieratic
topics.short: Letters, accounts, legal records, literature and religious texts were written in hieratic on papyrus, wood and ostraca.
topics.trouble: Students think most Egyptian writing was carved. Most of it was written in ink, in hieratic.

topics.title: Reading Hieratic
topics.short: Egyptologists read hieratic by transcribing it, sign by sign, into hieroglyphs, then transliterating.
topics.trouble: Students think hieratic is a separate language. It is the same language in a faster hand.

topics.title: Late Egyptian
topics.short: Late Egyptian, the everyday language of the New Kingdom, uses articles (pꜣ, tꜣ, nꜣ) and new verb forms.
topics.trouble: Students think Middle Egyptian vanished in the New Kingdom. It stayed in use for formal texts beside Late Egyptian.

topics.title: Late Egyptian Texts
topics.short: Late Egyptian texts include letters, the tomb-robbery papyri, the story of Wenamun and love poems.
topics.trouble: Students date all stories to the Middle Kingdom. Many lively stories are Late Egyptian.

topics.title: The Demotic Script
topics.short: Demotic grew out of hieratic in the 7th century BC; it is very cursive, written right to left, with many signs joined.
topics.trouble: Students confuse Demotic with Greek on the Rosetta Stone. Demotic is the middle text, an Egyptian script.

topics.title: Demotic Texts
topics.short: Demotic was used for contracts, letters, tax receipts and stories like the tales of Setne Khamwas.
topics.trouble: Students think Demotic was only for business. It also has a rich literature.

topics.title: Demotic on the Rosetta Stone
topics.short: The Demotic text of the Rosetta Stone (32 lines) is the best preserved of its Egyptian texts and was key to Young's work.
topics.trouble: Students think the hieroglyphic part is the longest. It is the most damaged: only 14 lines survive.

topics.title: Where Coptic Comes From
topics.short: Coptic is the last stage of Egyptian, written from about the 3rd century AD by Egyptian Christians in Greek letters plus letters from Demotic.
topics.trouble: Students think Coptic is a separate language from ancient Egyptian. It is Egyptian, written in a new alphabet.

topics.title: The Coptic Alphabet
topics.short: Coptic uses the 24 Greek letters, from alpha to omega, for Egyptian sounds.
topics.trouble: Students read Coptic with Greek sounds for every letter. Some letters are mostly used in Greek loanwords.

topics.title: The Letters from Demotic
topics.short: Sahidic Coptic adds six letters from Demotic, ϣ ϥ ϩ ϫ ϭ ϯ, for sounds Greek lacked; Bohairic adds ϧ.
topics.trouble: Students mistake ϣ (sh) for the Greek omega ω. Look for the tail.

topics.title: What Coptic Tells Us
topics.short: Because Coptic writes vowels, it shows how Egyptian words sounded late in their history: rn "name" is ⲣⲁⲛ, ran.
topics.trouble: Students apply Coptic vowels to Old Egyptian. Pronunciation changed over three thousand years.

topics.title: Coptic Dialects and Coptic Today
topics.short: Coptic had dialects, chiefly Sahidic in the south and Bohairic in the north; Bohairic is still used in Coptic Church services.
topics.trouble: Students think Coptic died out completely. It survives in the worship of the Coptic Church.

topics.title: The Last Hieroglyphic Inscription
topics.short: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae on 24 August AD 394, beside a figure of the god Mandulis.
topics.trouble: Students date the end of hieroglyphs to Cleopatra. They were carved for more than four centuries after her.

topics.title: The Last Demotic
topics.short: The last dated Demotic inscription, also at Philae, comes from AD 452.
topics.trouble: Students think hieroglyphs outlasted Demotic. Demotic lasted about sixty years longer.

topics.title: Meroitic, the Script of Kush
topics.short: The kingdom of Kush wrote its own language in Meroitic script; its sounds were worked out in 1909, but much of the language is still not understood.
topics.trouble: Students think being able to read a script means understanding it. Meroitic can be sounded out, but its meaning is only partly known.
